summary.text: Take \(n=7\). Since the prescribed set forces \(x\ge 3\) and \(x\le y\le z\), any such triple would satisfy \(x+y+z\ge 3x\ge 9\), contradicting \(x+y+z=7\); thus the “moreover” clause already fails before primality is considered.

full_proof.text:
Let an admissible representation of an integer \(n\) mean a triple of positive integers
\[
x\le y\le z,\qquad x+y+z=n,
\]
for which all six integers
\[
2x-1,\quad 2y-1,\quad 2z-1,\quad 2xy-1,\quad 2xz-1,\quad 2yz-1
\]
are prime. The conjecture asserts both that every \(n>5\) has at least one admissible representation and, moreover, that for every \(n>6\) one can choose such a representation with
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]

The “moreover” assertion already fails at \(n=7\).

Indeed, suppose for contradiction that it held for \(n=7\). Since \(7>6\), there would be positive integers \(x,y,z\) such that
\[
x+y+z=7,
\]
with
\[
x\le y\le z
\]
and
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\},
\]
as well as the six required primality conditions.

Membership in the displayed five-element set gives the exhaustive alternatives
\[
x=3,\quad x=4,\quad x=6,\quad x=10,\quad\text{or}\quad x=15.
\]
In every case, \(x\ge 3\).

The ordering gives \(y\ge x\), and by transitivity \(z\ge y\ge x\), so in particular \(z\ge x\). Consequently,
\[
x+y+z\ge x+x+x=3x.
\]
Using \(x+y+z=7\), this yields
\[
3x\le 7.
\]
On the other hand, \(x\ge3\) implies
\[
3x\ge 3\cdot3=9.
\]
Combining the two inequalities gives
\[
9\le 3x\le7,
\]
which is impossible.

Thus there is no ordered positive triple \(x\le y\le z\) summing to \(7\) whose first entry belongs to \(\{3,4,6,10,15\}\). This obstruction occurs before any primality condition is considered, so the primality requirements cannot remedy it. Hence the required restricted representation does not exist for \(n=7>6\), and the “moreover” clause is false. Since that clause is part of the combined conjecture, the conjecture about A229969 as stated is disproved.
